title: Traps: the claim and the correction
scope: These challenges isolate false extensions. Their related proofs, identities and exact counterexamples retain their own evidence status. None of the 46 atlas entries is reclassified as a trap.

entries.title: Does a flat tangent return every point?
entries.claim: At r = 1 + √6, the fourth-return displacement has zero derivative at the two-cycle points. Therefore four logistic updates return every starting point exactly.
entries.correction: The local derivative identity is true. The global conclusion is false: the nonlinear fourth iterate is a degree-16 polynomial, not the identity on an interval.
proof: Let f(x) = r x(1 − x), with r = 1 + √6. The two cycle slopes are −1 − √2 and −1 + √2. Their product is −1, so the derivative of the fourth iterate is 1 at either cycle point and the derivative of its displacement is zero there.

The leading coefficient of f is −r. Composing once more sends a leading coefficient a to −r a². Four compositions therefore have degree 16 and leading coefficient −r¹⁵, which is nonzero. Such a polynomial cannot agree with x on an interval.
An explicit starting point gives f⁴(1/2) − 1/2 = 1021(1 − √6)/65536, which is nonzero. Here f⁴ means fourfold composition, not the fourth power of a function value.
preservedFacts: The cycle Lyapunov exponent per original update is ½ log|−1| = 0.
The paired linear-response matrix satisfies C² = −I and C⁴ = I.
The later cubic calculation supplies a separate local attraction result.

entries.title: Does the Möbius sign certify twins?
entries.claim: If μ(m² − 1) = +1 and μ(m²) = 0, then m − 1 and m + 1 must both be prime.
entries.correction: The implication from twin primes to this sign pattern is true. Its converse is false. The exact counterexample at m = 34 remains a mathematical treasure.
proof: Set m = 34. Then m² − 1 = 1155 = 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 is squarefree with four prime factors, so μ(1155) = +1. The next integer is 34², so μ(1156) = 0.
Nevertheless, m − 1 = 33 = 3 × 11 and m + 1 = 35 = 5 × 7 are both composite. Thus the required sign pattern holds while the claimed conclusion fails.
For integers m ≥ 3, the stronger condition Ω(m² − 1) = 2 is equivalent to both neighbours being prime: Ω is additive on the product (m − 1)(m + 1), and both factors are at least two.
formulaText: For m ≥ 3: Ω(m² − 1) = 2 ⇔ both neighbours are prime
preservedFacts: Twin primes do imply the adjacent Möbius pattern (+1, 0).
The m = 34 counterexample is an exact refutation of the converse.
The Ω = 2 characterization retains its stated domain m ≥ 3.

entries.title: Do two bases remain at the summit?
entries.claim: Every upper height from just above one through the maximum, including the maximum itself, is attained by two distinct finite real bases.
entries.correction: Two distinct bases exist only strictly below the maximum. At the maximum height the inverse branches meet, leaving exactly one finite real base.
proof: For u = c^(−v), v = c^u and c > 1, set t = v log c. The exact identity v log v = t exp(−t) reduces the question to a single curve.
Its derivative is exp(−t)(1 − t). The unique maximum 1/e occurs at t = 1, so the maximum height v_max = exp(W₀(1/e)) has only that one value of t.
Recovering c = exp(t/v) gives the unique base c_peak = exp(1/v_max). Interior heights 1 < v < v_max have two bases; heights above the maximum and height one have none among finite c > 1.
formulaText: At the maximum: t = 1, so exactly one finite base
preservedFacts: The full convergence result remains valid for every real c > 1.
Every strict interior height has exactly two distinct finite bases.
The maximum height is attained; c_peak is not a largest permitted base.
